ℹ️ gills on hymenium, free, dense, initially pinkish, turning brown and then dark chocolate brown as the mushroom matures

🟤 spore print is brown
🛣️ ecology is saprotrophic, often found in urban and disturbed habitats such as roadside verges and gardens, as well as grasslands

ℹ️ Stipe: Slender, more or less equal, surface dry, initially whitish or pale, becoming powdery orangish-brown, basal mycelium white
⚪ Spore print white
🍄 Parasitic on decaying mushrooms (Russula, Lactarius spp.), appears when the host has begun to blacken and decay, singly, groups in mixed, hardwood, coniferous forests, summer through autumn

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Recognizable by its utricular sporangia, the Badhamia utricularis slime mold can be found on rotting wood and leaves. Its lifecycle is captivating, shifting from amoeba-like cells, grouping to form a slug-like mass, and eventually becoming the fruiting body. As a decomposer, it helps recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems, and its distinct sporangia offer a fascinating study for mycologists and naturalists alike.

As a decomposer, it helps recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems, and its distinct sporangia offer a fascinating study for mycologists and naturalists alike.

🔤 Recognizable by its utricular sporangia, the Badhamia utricularis slime mold can be found on rotting wood and leaves. Its lifecycle is captivating, shifting from amoeba-like cells, grouping to form a slug-like mass, and eventually becoming the fruiting body. As a decomposer, it helps recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems, and its distinct sporangia offer a fascinating study for mycologists and naturalists alike.

ℹ️ Hymenium: Pores small, rounded, lemon-yellow when young, later to olive-yellow, rapidly bruising blue when touched

🌳 Ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved trees: oak, beech, hornbeam, chestnut and lime; woodland, parks and calcareous or base-rich soils; summer to early autumn
🤢 Strongly inedible, extremely bitter, causes severe gastrointestinal symptoms
📏 Fruit body: Large and robust; stipe ~5–10 cm long, ~3–5 cm thick
📐 Cap: ∅ ~7–20(–30) cm
🔪 Flesh pale yellow to whitish, rapidly turning blue when cut or bruised
🧪 KOH orange on flesh; red-brown on cap
👃 Pleasant, mushroomy
👅 Strongly bitter
🔬 Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, ~11.5–14 × 4–5.5 µm; pileipellis a trichodermium of interwoven septate, finely incrusted hyphae
🔤 Large pale rooting bolete with yellow pores that bruise blue, bitter taste and reticulation

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Easily recognized by its large, round to pear-shaped fruiting body that can reach impressive sizes. The inside (gleba) is initially solid and white, becoming yellowish and finally olive-brown as it matures. When fully mature, the puffball releases its spores through an opening or when the fruiting body is disrupted. This species is edible when young, and the interior flesh is completely white. However, it becomes inedible as it matures and the spores develop, turning the flesh into a mass of olive-brown powder. Always ensure the flesh is pure white throughout before consumption, as other, inedible or toxic puffball species can appear similar when young.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Recognizable by its semicircular, fan-shaped cap that bears dark brown scales on a lighter background. The underside contains small pores rather than gills, where it releases its spores. This mushroom is found on dead logs or living trees, where it can act as a decomposer or a parasite. While edible, only the younger specimens are recommended for consumption as the older ones can be quite tough and have a strong flavor. The smell of a fresh specimen is often compared to watermelon rind. As always, proper identification is crucial as there are many species of Polypores, and not all of them are edible.

🔤 Recognizable by its semicircular, fan-shaped cap that bears dark brown scales on a lighter background. The underside contains small pores rather than gills, where it releases its spores. This mushroom is found on dead logs or living trees, where it can act as a decomposer or a parasite. While edible, only the younger specimens are recommended for consumption as the older ones can be quite tough and have a strong flavor. The smell of a fresh specimen is often compared to watermelon rind. As always, proper identification is crucial as there are many species of Polypores, and not all of them are edible.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Commonly known as ergot, is a parasitic fungus that infects grasses, especially rye. The fungus replaces the grains of the host plant with hard, dark purple to black sclerotia, which contain toxic alkaloids. These sclerotia are the overwintering stage and germinate to produce fruiting bodies that release ascospores. During the growing season, the fungus also produces conidia in a sticky honeydew that spreads the infection.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Commonly known as ergot, is a parasitic fungus that infects grasses, especially rye. The fungus replaces the grains of the host plant with hard, dark purple to black sclerotia, which contain toxic alkaloids. These sclerotia are the overwintering stage and germinate to produce fruiting bodies that release ascospores. During the growing season, the fungus also produces conidia in a sticky honeydew that spreads the infection.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Diminutive mushroom which often appears in dense clusters on decaying wood. Its delicate, almost transparent stature and creamy-white caps make it easily distinguishable from other inky cap species. As with other members of its genus, the gills will "deliquesce" or turn into an inky black liquid as they mature, a mechanism for spore dispersal.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Easily recognized mushroom due to its tall, white, shaggy cap, which turns black and begins to dissolve from the bottom up as it matures. This process of liquefying gills is known as deliquescence. It's a popular edible mushroom, best eaten when young and while the gills are still white or pink. The taste is mild and not distinctive. Note that like other members of the Coprinus genus, it should not be consumed with alcohol as it can cause adverse reactions.

🌲💧🌾 Conifer dominant forest, within young spruces, deep in wet moss (Hylocomium splendens)

ℹ️ Hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; bright carmine to blood-red when young, becoming rusty red-brown with maturity
ℹ️ Cap: Convex to broadly convex, later plane, often with a broad umbo; hygrophanous, finely silky-fibrillose; rich blood-red, dark red to dull reddish-brown
ℹ️ Hymenium Attachment: Adnate
ℹ️ Stipe: Slender, cylindrical, blood-red to dark red; orange-yellow to reddish-yellow basal mycelium; cortina red and ephemeral; ring absent
🟤🟠 Spore print rusty brown
🌲🌾 Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce; mesic to damp mossy coniferous forests, often among Sphagnum and bilberry on nutrient-rich ground; scattered or gregariously; late summer to autumn
😒 Not recommended; considered inedible
⚕️ Anthraquinone pigments including emodin, dermocybin, dermolutein and dermorubin

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Fungus that forms large, bracket-like or hoof-shaped fruiting bodies on trees. The top surface is typically glossy and zonate with bands of different colors, ranging from white to red-brown to almost black. The underside contains many small pores where the spores are released. It's often found on dead or dying trees, where it can act as a decomposer (saprotrophic) or weak parasite. Although it's not poisonous, it's considered inedible due to its tough, woody texture. It has been used traditionally in some cultures for medicinal purposes.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Remarkable mushroom due to its decurrent, bright yellow pores which undergo a color change to blue-grey when bruised. It holds a close taxonomic relation to the genus Paxillus. Its primary habitat is in Europe, forming a symbiotic mycorrhizal association with alders, although reports also indicate its presence in regions such as China, Japan, and California. Notably different from the typical boletes, this mushroom stands out both for its unique association with alder and its distinct pore coloration.

Its primary habitat is in Europe, forming a symbiotic mycorrhizal association with alders, although reports also indicate its presence in regions such as China, Japan, and California. Notably different from the typical boletes, this mushroom stands out both for its unique association with alder and its distinct pore coloration.

It is not considered edible and often renders the host mushroom inedible as well.

🏥🛣️🌲🍂 City zone nearby pine dominant forest, withing Pinus sylvestris trees, on grassland with conifer litter

ℹ️ Hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; whitish to cream when young, becoming pinkish-buff to pale ochre
ℹ️ Cap: Convex when young, later broadly flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, dry to slightly glossy; vivid orange, orange-red to orange-brown; unzoned, margin initially inrolled
ℹ️ Hymenium Attachment: Broadly adnate to shortly decurrent
ℹ️ Stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, smooth, orange-brown to yellow-orange, usually paler near apex; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
⚪🟡 Spore print ivory to pale cream
🌲🌳 Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and pine, occasionally birch and other hardwoods; coniferous and mixed forests, often on acidic soils; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
😒 Edibility disputed; generally not recommended
📏 Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2.5–7 cm long and ~0.5–1.2 cm thick
📐 Cap ∅ ~1–5(–7) cm
🔪 Whitish to pale orange, brittle; abundant white latex unchanging, mild
🧪 Guaiac grey-green; FeSO₄ grey-green on flesh
👃 Faint, slightly unpleasant, rubbery
👅 Mild, slightly bitter, radish-like
🔬 Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, ~7–9.5 × 6–7.5 µm, ornamented with low amyloid warts and connecting ridges; numerous fusoid cystidia
🔤 Small vivid orange milkcap with immutable white latex

🌳💧🍂🍃 Wooded meadow nature reserve, under oak, birch, aspen trees, in damp grassy soil with decaying leaves remains

ℹ️ Hymenium: Gills fairly crowded; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming pale buff with age
ℹ️ Cap: Convex when young, later flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, viscid to slimy when fresh; pale violet-grey, lilac-grey to buff-brown, darkening with age; unzoned or faintly zoned
ℹ️ Hymenium Attachment: Adnate to shortly decurrent
ℹ️ Stipe: Cylindrical, pale cream to whitish, smooth, sometimes slightly viscid when young; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
⚪🟡 Spore print pale cream to pale yellowish
🌳💧 Mycorrhizal mainly with birch and willow; damp woodland, bog margins and mossy acidic soils; solitary to gregariously; summer to autumn
😒 Not recommended; bitter, regarded as potentially poisonous
📏 Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.6–2.5 cm thick
📐 Cap ∅ ~3–10 cm
🔪 Whitish to buff, firm and brittle; white latex and exposed flesh slowly stain lilac
🧪 KOH green on cap surface
👃 Faintly fruity, indistinct
👅 Mild initially to bitter
🔬 Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, ~7.5–11 × 6.5–8.5 µm, ornamented with amyloid broad ridges ~0.5–1 µm high forming an incomplete reticulum; pleuro- and cheilomacrocystidia fusiform to subventricose; pileipellis an ixocutis
🔤 Slimy lilac-grey milkcap with white latex staining intensely violet-purple

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Small agaric that is often found in troops or fairy rings in grassy areas. It is characterized by its small, buff-colored, bell-shaped cap and the spaced gills on the underside. The flesh is thin but tough. It's popular in cooking, particularly in French cuisine, where it's known as "mousseron". It can be eaten fresh, but its flavor greatly intensifies when dried, making it an excellent mushroom for flavoring dishes.

ℹ️ Hymenium: Smooth to slightly uneven, vivid orange to orange-red or vermilion
ℹ️ Apothecium: Sessile, initially cup-shaped, later shallowly saucer- to disc-shaped; exterior paler orange to reddish-brown, finely pubescent; margin dotted with short inconspicuous brown hairs
ℹ️ Stipe: Absent
⚪ Spore print white
🌱🍂 Saprobic on damp bare, mossy or sandy soil; forests, woodland tracks, roadsides and disturbed ground; scattered to gregarious; summer to autumn
😒 Tiny and no culinary value
📏 Fruit body very small; apothecia ~1–2 mm tall
📐 Apothecium ∅ ~2–15 mm
🔪 Orange-red, thin, waxy and brittle, unchanging when cut
🔍 Paraphyses filiform with enlarged orange-pigmented apices; marginal hairs brown, blunt, septate, up to ~200 µm long
🔬 Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline, biguttulate, ~16–20 × 9–11 µm excluding ornamentation; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~215–300 × 11–15 µm, inamyloid;
🔤 Tiny vivid orange-red soil cup with short brown marginal hairs

As always, it's essential to properly identify any wild mushrooms before considering them for consumption, as many species can look similar but have vastly different edibility profiles.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Characterized by its yellow or ochre cap and white gills and stem. Like other members of the Russula genus, it has a brittle texture. This species forms a mycorrhizal relationship with various trees, and it is often found in coniferous and deciduous forests. It's known for its mild, nutty flavor and is considered a good edible mushroom. As always, proper identification is crucial as there are many species in the Russula genus, some of which may be inedible or have a peppery or bitter taste.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Mushroom known for its large size, robust stature, and uniformly white appearance. Like other members of the Russula genus, it has a brittle texture due to the presence of spherical cells called sphaerocysts. It can often be found in association with various trees as it forms mutualistic mycorrhizal relationships. While it is considered edible, its flavor is mild and not particularly remarkable, and some individuals find it slightly bitter. It's always important to be cautious when identifying Russula species, as some can be very similar in appearance but have different edibility profiles.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Russula fragilis exhibits a relatively high level of spore ornamentation, featuring warts that are isolated or only infrequently connected by lines. The gills of this species contain predominantly 4-spored basidia, contributing to its overall spore density. Additionally, it possesses intracellular pigments, which result in its vivid cap colors. This species is noted for its sensitivity to environmental conditions, particularly soil pH, favoring more acidic substrates. It is subject to parasitization by the fungus Hypomyces lactifluorum, which transforms it into the "Lobster Mushroom." Studies have shown that Russula fragilis has a high degree of mycorrhizal specificity, most commonly forming associations with members of the Pinaceae family.

❌ Stipe: Lacking.
❌ Not applicable, spores are released directly from the ascomata

⚠️ Not edible
📏 Fruit body size individual ascomata are very small, 0.05–0.1 mm in diameter
🧪 No significant reactions with common reagents
👃 Odour indistinct
🔬 Ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline, measuring 7–10 × 2–3 µm, asci 8-spored

science.raw:
ℹ️ Hymenium: Smooth, without pores or gills; pale cream, buff to ochraceous; fresh surface characteristically stains bright yellow when scratched or bruised
ℹ️ Cap: Fan- to semicircular, thin and leathery, overlapping in tiers; concentrically zoned grey-yellow, ochre, buff to pale brown; finely velvety to tomentose, sometimes greenish from algae with age; margin thin and wavy
ℹ️ Hymenium Attachment: Smooth fertile surface covers the underside
ℹ️ Stipe: Absent; usually attached by a relatively narrow lateral base
⚪🟤 Spore print white to very pale brown
🌳🪵 Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood trunks and branches; overlapping clusters; fruit bodies persistent year-round, sporulating summer to autumn
🪵 Inedible; tough, leathery and tasteless
📏 Fruit body small to medium; flesh ~1–2 mm thick
📐 Cap width ~3–7 cm
🔪 Beige to ochraceous, thin, tough and leathery; fertile surface bruises distinctly yellow
🧪 No macroscopic reagents reaction
👃 Indistinct
👅 Tasteless
🔬 Spores cylindrical to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~5.5–8 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; thick-walled pseudocystidia present;
🔤 Zoned velvety hardwood curtain crust with a yellow-bruising smooth underside

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Mushroom characterized by a smooth, often sticky cap and yellowish tubes under the cap. It is particularly noted for the droplets (or "weeping") that appear at the base of the tubes, which gives the mushroom its common name. It forms a mycorrhizal relationship with pine trees, helping the trees to absorb water and nutrients while receiving sugars and other nutrients in return. While edible, it's not typically considered a top-tier culinary mushroom due to its somewhat slimy texture. Nevertheless, it can be a nice addition to dishes when cooked properly, and some recommend removing the skin of the cap to improve the texture.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Mushroom recognized by its distinctive cap with a variegated pattern of reddish-brown and yellow hues. Like other members of the Suillus genus, it has tubes instead of gills under the cap, which help to identify it as a bolete. It forms mutualistic relationships with pine trees, helping the tree to absorb nutrients while the mushroom benefits from the tree's photosynthesis products. Although it is edible, the cap's skin should be removed before cooking, as it can cause indigestion in some people.

🔤 Mushroom recognized by its distinctive cap with a variegated pattern of reddish-brown and yellow hues. Like other members of the Suillus genus, it has tubes instead of gills under the cap, which help to identify it as a bolete. It forms mutualistic relationships with pine trees, helping the tree to absorb nutrients while the mushroom benefits from the tree's photosynthesis products. Although it is edible, the cap's skin should be removed before cooking, as it can cause indigestion in some people.

traits.label: Overview
traits.text: Plant pathogenic fungus that specifically infects bird cherry (Prunus padus) leaves, causing characteristic 'pocket galls'. These are pouch-like deformities that occur on the leaves and are the result of the fungus manipulating the plant tissue. Taphrina padi belongs to the Ascomycota division, and its primary mode of reproduction is through the production of ascospores. This fungus is mainly of interest for its effect on bird cherry trees and is not used for culinary or medicinal purposes.

🌡️ 16°C 🌦️ Sprinkles, scattered clouds 💨 Wind 230° SW->NE, 15 km/h
🌎 Vabaõhukooli tee, Tallinn, Harju, Eesti 
📌 59°27'52.7"N 24°52'57.3"E
🚣‍♂️🌳🪵 Deciduous  forest, near river, on dead dried hardwood branch

ℹ️ Hymenium: Pores round to slightly angular, cream to pale ochre; ~3–4 per mm
ℹ️ Cap: Semicircular to shell-shaped, often overlapping in tiers; concentrically zoned ochre, buff, orange-brown to grey-brown; alternating finely tomentose, velvety and smoother zones; margin thin and paler
ℹ️ Hymenium Attachment: Pore surface covers the underside of the bracket
ℹ️ Stipe: Absent; broadly attached and sessile
⚪ Spore print white
🌳🪵 Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood, especially beech and oak; fallen trunks, branches, stumps and standing dead wood; overlapping clusters; annual but persistent, visible year-round
🪵 Inedible; tough, leathery and corky
📏 Fruit body small to medium; often forming much larger overlapping masses
📐 Cap width ~1.5–5(–6) cm
🔪 White to cream, tough-fibrous and corky, unchanging when cut
🧪 No macroscopic reagents reaction
👃 Indistinct
👅 Indistinct
🔬 Spores cylindrical to slightly curved/allantoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5.5–8 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent
🔤 Ochre-zoned hardwood bracket with broad hairy bands and cream pores

🌲🌾 Pine-spruce-birch-juniper wooded heath, on dry conifer stump
🍄 Tubiferaceae / Myxogastria

ℹ️ Plasmodium Phase: The active, feeding phase appears as a moist, slimy, gelatinous mass, usually pale pink to reddish, slowly moving across decaying wood and consuming microorganisms
ℹ️ Fruiting Bodies: Forms dense, crowded, cushion-shaped to cylindrical sporangia, initially bright pink to red, transitioning to orange, rust-red, or dark brown as they mature, with a dry, granular surface
🟤🟠 Spore mass powdery and rusty-brown in mature fruiting bodies
🌲🍂 Saprobic, found on decaying logs, stumps, and wood debris, late spring to autumn, favoring moist, shaded environments
⚠️ Inedible
📏 Fruiting body individual sporangia are 2–20 mm long and 1–2 mm wide, entire clusters may span several centimeters across
👃 Odour indistinct or slightly earthy
🔬 Spores spherical, finely warted, 6–8 µm, interconnected by a capillitium network
🔤 Strikingly vibrant slime mold that transitions from gelatinous pink plasmodium to dense, colorful fruiting masses

science.raw:
ℹ️ Hymenium: Perithecia embedded in the black stromatic surface, appearing as minute pimple-like bumps with ostioles; white powdery conidia produced externally during the asexual stage
ℹ️ Fruit body: Erect, slender, cylindrical to flattened, often forked or antler-like; black, finely hairy near base, with conspicuous white powdery tips when young; becoming entirely charcoal-black and minutely roughened at maturity
ℹ️ Stipe: Short to elongated, black, tough and wiry, sometimes longitudinally grooved; base broadened and covered with dark brown to black tomentum
⚪⚫ Spore mass white from asexual conidia, dark brown to black from mature ascospores
🌳🪵 Saprobic, causing soft rot on decaying hardwood; fallen branches, stumps, logs and buried woody debris; scattered to densely clustered; year-round
🪵 Inedible; tough, rubbery and insubstantial

📐 Perithecia ∅ ~0.4–0.7 mm
🔪 White to cream internally, solid, tough and elastic, unchanging when cut
🧪 Amyloid apical ring turning blue in Melzer's reagent
🔬 Ascospores ellipsoid to bean-shaped, inequilateral, smooth, brown, ~9.5–13.5 × 4.5–6 µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~140–220 µm long; conidia hyaline, smooth, narrowly fusiform-clavate, ~8.5–12 × 3.5–4 µm
